h1: How to taste your own homebrew honestly and improve it
title: Taste Your Own Homebrew Honestly | Craft Beer School
desc: How to judge your own homebrew without bias: blind tasting, a simple scoresheet, comparing with commercial beers and turning notes into changes.
teaser: Every brewer thinks their own beer is good. The trick is finding out what it actually tastes like.
standfirst: You made it, so you like it. That is the problem. Here is how to taste your own beer as a stranger would, find what is really wrong and change the next batch because of it.
sections: Why your own beer fools you

Brewers are the worst judges of their own beer. You know what you meant it to taste like, so your brain fills in the gaps. You remember the effort, so you forgive the faults. Friends are polite, so they say it is great.

None of that helps you improve. The aim of honest tasting is simple: find the one or two things that would make the next batch better, then change them.

Taste under the same conditions every time, so differences come from the beer and not the setting.

  • Clean glass. Rinse a clean glass with plain water. Detergent residue kills head and aroma.
  • Right temperature. Too cold hides flavour and faults. Most ales show best around 8 to 12 °C, lagers a little colder.
  • Neutral room. No cooking smells, incense or perfume. Not straight after spicy food.
  • Small pours. 100 ml is enough to judge. Spit or tip the rest if you are tasting several beers.

The single best way to remove bias is not knowing which beer is yours. Ask a friend to pour your beer and a commercial example of the same style into identical glasses and mark them underneath. Taste both, note your thoughts, then reveal.

A triangle test goes further. Pour three glasses, two of one beer and one of the other. If you cannot pick the odd one out reliably, the difference you were worried about may be smaller than you think. It is how commercial panels check whether a recipe change can actually be tasted.

Writing things down forces you to be specific. You do not need a complex form. Work through four headings in order:

  1. Appearance. Colour, clarity, head size and how long it lasts.
  2. Aroma. Malt, hops, yeast character and anything that should not be there.
  3. Flavour. Sweetness, bitterness, balance and finish.
  4. Mouthfeel. Body, carbonation, warmth, astringency.

Score each heading out of five if numbers help you. The total matters less than the pattern across batches. A beer that scores well on aroma but always drops points on mouthfeel tells you where to look.

Then answer one question: is this beer what I set out to brew? The BJCP scoresheet adds structure if you want it. Our guide to the BJCP scoresheet walks through each section. A shared vocabulary like the beer flavour wheel helps you name what you find.

Many problems in homebrew come from a short list of faults. Butter or butterscotch points to diacetyl, often from rushing fermentation. Green apple suggests acetaldehyde, usually a beer bottled too early. Cooked sweetcorn is DMS, from a weak or covered boil. Wet cardboard means oxidation. Medicinal or plastic notes often come from chlorine in the water or from wild yeast.

Our guide to beer off flavours explains where each one comes from. Knowing the cause tells you which part of your process to change.

Taste at more than one point too. A beer at two weeks in the bottle, at six weeks and at three months can be three different beers. Hop aroma fades, malt rounds out and any oxidation shows itself. Keep two or three bottles from each batch back for later tastings, so you learn how your beers age rather than only how they start.

One palate has blind spots. Some people cannot smell diacetyl at levels that others find obvious. Ask two or three friends to taste with you using the same headings. Encourage blunt feedback. Tell them you want faults, not compliments.

Homebrew clubs and competitions are even better. Judges give written scores and comments, often surprisingly detailed. Tasting should stay relaxed and moderate. You are judging beer, not drinking a session, so small pours and plenty of water are the rule.

Tasting only helps if it changes what you do next. After each tasting:

  • Pick the one or two biggest issues.
  • Trace each back to a step in your process.
  • Change one thing in the next batch.
  • Write it all in your brew log so you can compare later.

Our guide to keeping a brew log shows what to record. Over a few batches, your notes become a map of how each process change affects the glass.

The limit of self-taught tasting is calibration. Without reference samples, you cannot be sure that what you call diacetyl is what a trained taster would. That is the gap structured sensory training fills: tasting spiked samples until each fault has a name and a threshold you trust.
faqs: What temperature should I taste my homebrew at?
Most ales show best around 8 to 12 °C. Very cold beer hides both flavour and faults, so let it warm a little before judging.
How do I taste my own beer without bias?
Taste it blind against a commercial example of the same style, with a friend pouring both into identical glasses.
Is it worth entering a homebrew competition?
Yes, for the feedback. Judges give written scores and comments that are often more honest than friends will be.
